Finally, we evaluate 20th-century reconstructions of East Asian modernity, showing how Nishida Kitarō's "pure experience" (Nishida, 1990) and Mou Zongsan's defense of "intellectual intuition" (zhi de zhijue 智的直覺) and the summum bonum (yuan shan 圓善; Mou, 1971, 1985) overcome Kantian finitude and Kierkegaardian existential disjunction (Kierkegaard, 1987).

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Civilization (2nd edition).
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Human Civilization: A New Framework for AI Governance and Human Responsibility -/- This work presents an original technical-philosophical foundation for global artificial intelligence governance, developed from Harmondeg philosophy. It addresses a fundamental challenge in contemporary AI governance: the absence of a sufficiently shared civilizational foundation capable of guiding technological development across diverse cultures, civilizations, religious beliefs, and philosophical traditions. -/- The publication comprises two interconnected essays. -/- The first, Artificial Intelligence Is Extending Beyond the Boundaries of Existing Governance, examines the structural limitations of prevailing AI governance approaches and argues that effective governance must be grounded in a coherent understanding of human civilization, ethical responsibility, and the relationship between technological capability and its consequences. -/- The second, Artificial Intelligence and Human Civilization, advances a civilizational declaration establishing humanity's non-transferable responsibility for its own civilization. It articulates two foundational ethical anchors: human nature and ethical capacity as the enduring basis of civilization, and civilizational sustainability as a guiding ethical responsibility in the age of artificial intelligence. -/- Together, the two essays establish a philosophical basis from which innovative AI governance principles, institutional arrangements, and practically applicable governance frameworks can be developed. The framework positions artificial intelligence as an extension of human capability while affirming humanity's continuing responsibility for the direction, consequences, and sustainability of civilization. -/- Drawing upon Harmondeg's understanding of existence, relationality, and Corre-Response, this research seeks to establish a universally shareable foundation for AI governance that accommodates cultural and philosophical diversity while supporting coherent ethical orientation, institutional responsibility, and future governance development. -/- The work contributes a foundational philosophical perspective to international discussions on AI governance, offering a pathway from shared civilizational principles toward innovative, actionable, and globally relevant governance mechanisms.

items.title: A Metaphysical Discussion of the Stability of Meaning and the Question of Reality.
items.abstract: A meaning may become recognizable across occasions and consequential within an institution while the reality attributed to its referent remains disputed. This essay examines that difference through a provisional Generative–Relational (GR) distinction among questions of ultimate ontology, operative relational organization, and situated manifestation. Currency and belonging serve as contrasting examples of how symbolic forms, institutional conditions, and lived commitments interact. Drawing on social ontology, theories of symbolic power, and historically bounded cases of the euro transition and Hull-House, the analysis distinguishes constitutive grounds from causal effects, semantic persistence from historical identity, and institutional authority from normative legitimacy. It examines how inherited meanings can enable coordination while permitting contestation, how successor organizations can acquire divergent responsibilities, and why interpretive mobility need not imply a privileged metaphysical standpoint. The proposed evidential approach requires an account of a relation's organization and potential rival mechanisms before stronger claims about its efficacy or persistence are warranted. For future community design, the resulting orientation concerns dependable obligations, plural forms of participation, and revisable authority. Semantic stabilization can participate in making social relations consequential; further claims about ontology, identity, and justice require their own justification.

items.title: Linguo-semiotic analysis of English texts.
items.pub: Dissertation, University of Santiago de Compostela
items.abstract: The central research question of this thesis is what linguo-semiotic analysis is, how and where it can be applied. In pursuit of an answer, the study begins with the exploration of semiotics, examines key semiotic concepts and foundational terminology. From this basis, the thesis identifies linguo-semiotics as a major subfield within semiotics, offers a comprehensive definition and in-depth analysis of linguo-semiosis and linguo-semiotic analysis. Within this framework, linguistic signs are defined to be a synergic outcome of both informational and communicational linguo-semiosis. By applying the Peircean-Borges Signtree model as an analytic scaffolding to classify and trace sign functions among linguistic signs, the thesis demonstrates that linguistic signs possess a composite dynamic nature, and their interpretive reconfigurations depend on context, function, and cultural embedding.

items.title: Who Must Prevent the Next Reich? Extreme Injustice, Relational Realism and Global Legal Responsibility.
items.abstract: A constituent assembly elected with majority support strips native-born Brazilians defined by descent of their nationality and authorizes their expulsion. The research asks who may demand which conduct from which State, on what legal basis and before which irreversible moment. It argues that constitutional replacement extinguishes neither the State's international obligations nor the requirement to justify the deprivation to each person affected; that relational position identifies and grades the loss but does not by itself ground the obligation; and that third-party responsibility does not follow the gravity of the harm, depending instead on a legal link, on effective control over the means of protection and on a demonstrated source. Comparison with existing law, including the European Pact on Migration and Asylum, applicable since June 2026, and with Monica Hakimi's theory of specific protective duties shows that the link-based distribution of duties already has precedents. The residual contribution is procedural and temporal: two distinct treaty-based procedures are proposed, one for the timely review of data transfers capable of locating persecuted persons and another for urgent admission decisions tied to a last-resort allocation rule, both triggerable by those affected and subject to review. The research, theoretical and legal-doctrinal, tests each proposition through controlled variations and states the conditions under which it would fail.

items.title: Functionalism entails agnosticism about AI consciousness.
items.abstract: Can AI be conscious? A high-profile debate is currently unfolding between proponents of non-biological views and proponents of biological views. Whereas the latter argues that certain small-scale biological properties are necessary to instantiate consciousness, the former denies this fiercely, instead suggesting that the relevant properties are exclusively found at larger non-biological scales. Much attention is currently devoted to resolving this dispute. In this paper, I don’t address the dispute directly. Instead, I will pose a more fundamental problem that remains even if this dispute is resolved. Specifically, despite their disagreements, most researchers on both sides of the dispute adopt functionalism as their metaphysical scaffold to describe which properties are required to instantiate consciousness. However, I argue that if functionalism on either side is used as a metaphysical scaffold, then agnosticism about AI consciousness follows because of what I call the Functional Grain Problem: There are a plethora of functional individuations available for any candidate property, whether biological or non-biological, some of which imply that AI can be conscious, whereas other’s don’t, and neither scientific insights nor the central tenets of functionalism tells us anything about which individuations to go for. Because of this, neither large-scale functionalism (assumed by most non-biological views) nor small-scale functionalism (assumed by most biological views) have any obvious implications about the possibility of AI consciousness, despite a prevailing sentiment suggesting that they do. The result is that even if we figure out whether consciousness requires biology or not agnosticism about AI consciousness is still rationally mandated. I briefly analyze potential ways out of the agnostic predicament, suggesting that they are either problematic or undesirable, and I end the paper by comparing my arguments with other agnostic proposals.

items.title: Elaborations on Earlier Essays.
items.abstract: In this elaboration on Occam’s Moral Razor, I re-evaluate my tripartite moral framework—emotional resonance, rational accuracy, and pragmatism—via a process of reflective equilibrium and insights gained from real-world conflicts encountered while studying Gemmology. I examine structural tensions within the model, specifically where empathy and uncritical trust conflict with pragmatic survival in competitive, hostile or simply secretly unfamiliar environments. Additionally, by contrasting rigid, rule-based ethics with Moral Particularism, I argue that relying blindly on general moral rules creates dangerous blind spots, whereas ‘streetwise’ context-sensitive judgement is essential for navigating complex power dynamics. Additionally, elaborating on my essay regarding New Atheists, I demonstrate how subtle cognitive errors, such as subliminal pattern recognition, impair situational awareness—a matter possessing key implications for the currently hugely debated topic of online manipulation. Finally let me also mention that, whilst my essay is rather critical of a certain unnamed institution I refer to as 'the Club', it is obvious that my points are actually highly subjective and speculative. In fact, having pasted my essay into Gemini, its verdict was that my criticisms were extremely inaccurate and unfounded. The only reason I have not yet decided to remove the criticisms, is that they function as a very useful parable for the Moral Philosophy argument I want to make. My essay is in no way an empirically accurate assessment of the institution in question. In fact, the reader should interpret my mention of the Club as simply a useful fiction serving a role in an essay on moral philosophy. On a more general note let me add that I wrote my essay in haste and will likely make edits over coming weeks, especially regarding the complexities of moral philosophy.

items.title: The Anthropocentric Bias of Anthropic Reasoning: A Case of Implicit Dualism.
items.abstract: Methodological anthropic reasoning (MAR), popularized by Bostrom ([2002]), aims to correct for observation selection bias by appealing to observer-relative information. I show that MAR's inferential structure is not uniquely tied to observers but applies to any set of entities subject to selection uncertainty. By miscasting a general epistemic problem as uniquely anthropic, MAR obscures its metaphysical assumptions and bypasses established probabilistic methods. Once stripped of its observer-centric framing and functionally reduced, anthropic reasoning collapses into ad hoc inference—forcing a choice: either acknowledge the metaphysical specialness of observers or concede there is no reason to privilege one physical pattern over another.

items.title: Ten Powers and a Practice: The Core Emotion Framework, What the Evidence Shows So Far, and Three Predictions Ready to Test.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) holds that everyone has the same ten inner powers, grouped in the Head, Heart and Gut, none good or bad in itself. Distress, on this account, comes from emotional rigidity: a few powers fuse and suppress the rest. The remedy is practice, above all Emotional Cycling, which is said to restore the powers’ independence. This paper sets out the framework in its author’s own words and places it beside research on psychological flexibility, cognitive fusion, acceptance and regulatory flexibility. It then summarises the exploratory evidence so far: of eight results that test the framework’s stated claims in existing data, four were supported, two were mixed and two were not supported. The central practice has not yet been tested. Three predictions follow directly from the framework: practice widens the range of every power, practice loosens fusion in daily life, and a trained practitioner can identify which powers dominate. Ready designs are given, and researchers are invited to run them. -/- Keywords: Core Emotion Framework; emotional rigidity; Emotional Cycling; psychological flexibility; research agenda Displaying abstract.txt.

items.title: Fusion, Exhaustion and Anxiety Over Time: New Tests of the Core Emotion Framework in Open Daily-Life Data.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) holds that distress arises when inner powers fuse and lose their free movement. Earlier exploratory work tested eight of its stated claims. This note reports six further relations that the framework states in its own words and that two open experience-sampling datasets measure, plus five re-tests. Being caught up in one’s thoughts went with mental exhaustion within the same person (r = .30, 336 people). Most of the variation in being caught up lay within persons (59%), in line with the claim that fusion is temporary. Being caught up at one prompt predicted more anxiety at the next (b = .065, 241 people), the first test of the time order the framework describes. Acceptance went with calm (r = .14) and confidence (r = .17), but not with sadness as stated (r = −.06). All published results were reproduced exactly. The effects are small to moderate and depend on matching questionnaire items to powers. -/- Keywords: Core Emotion Framework; cognitive fusion; experience sampling; anxiety; acceptance Displaying abstract.txt.

items.title: Normativity of Meaning Contextualised: A Davidsonian Account.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel contextualist account of the normativity of meaning, grounded in Davidsonian metasemantics. It presents the view that the normativity of meaning can arise not from global conventions or prescriptive rules, but from the local evidence-based practice under the constitutive ideal of rationality. By analysing how we achieve what Davidson called ‘first’ meaning, the paper demonstrates how context-local standards emerge within the boundaries set by the principle of charity. This framework preserves semantic systematicity and stability, and explains phenomena such as idiosyncrasy and linguistic mistakes without appealing to conventionalism, thereby breaking out of the dilemma between weak ‘correctness’ and overly strong ‘prescriptive’ construals of the normativity of meaning. The result is a robustly normative, yet moderately anti-conventionalist theory of meaning, which does not rule out the existence of linguistic conventions but rather takes their role to be far less significant.

items.title: Veränderung aus der Perspektive der Theorie der Einheitsbildung; Teil 7.
items.abstract: Der siebte Teil des Gesamtwerks untersucht, wie wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis Veränderun-gen verständlich macht und unter welchen Bedingungen sich wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis selbst weiterentwickeln und verbessern kann. Ausgangspunkt ist die Theorie der Einheitsbil-dung, nach der das Individuum seine Wirklichkeit nicht als bereits vollständig geordnete Welt vorfindet, sondern unter den Wirkungen einer unabhängig bestehenden Realität durch Unterscheidung, Verknüpfung und Stabilisierung erfahrbarer Zusammenhänge bildet. Die vorausgehenden Teile haben auf dieser Grundlage erklärt, wie Gegenstände und Beziehun-gen wiedererkannt, Veränderungen verstanden und ihre Entstehungsbedingungen untersucht werden können. Daran schließt sich die Frage an, wodurch sich wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis vom alltäglichen Verstehen unterscheidet, weshalb ihre Ergebnisse besondere Geltung bean-spruchen können und wann Veränderungen wissenschaftlicher Theorien tatsächlich einen Erkenntnisfortschritt darstellen. Kapitel 20 untersucht die wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis von Veränderung. Es wird begründet, dass Wissenschaft keine vom individuellen Verstehen unabhängige Erkenntnisfähigkeit vo-raussetzt, sondern dessen grundlegende Leistungen durch genauere Begriffsbildung, syste-matische Beobachtung, Messung und methodische Prüfung weiterentwickelt. Dabei wird zwischen der Feststellung einer Veränderung und der Erklärung ihres Zustandekommens unterschieden. Unterschiedliche wissenschaftliche Verfahren ermöglichen es, Veränderun-gen mathematisch zu beschreiben, ihre Ursachen zu untersuchen oder ihre Bedeutung inner-halb umfassenderer Zusammenhänge zu erklären. Die besondere Leistung wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis besteht darin, dass ihre Aussagen unter ausdrücklich bestimmten Bedingungen nachvollzogen, überprüft und gegebenenfalls korrigiert werden können. Auf dieser Grundla-ge wird wissenschaftliche Systemobjektivität als eine Form organisationsübergreifender Geltung begründet, die auf der methodisch kontrollierten Zusammenarbeit und gegenseiti-gen Überprüfung individueller Erkenntnisleistungen beruht. Kapitel 21 richtet die Untersuchung auf die Veränderung wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis selbst. Wissenschaftliche Begriffe, Methoden und Theorien können erweitert, verändert oder durch andere Erklärungszusammenhänge ersetzt werden. Nicht jede solche Veränderung bedeutet jedoch bereits einen Erkenntnisfortschritt. Entscheidend ist vielmehr, ob neue Er-kenntnisse genauere Bestimmungen …

items.title: Change from the Perspektive of the Unity Formation; Part VII.
items.abstract: The seventh part of the overall work examines how scientific knowledge makes changes intelligible and under what conditions scientific knowledge itself can develop and improve. Its point of departure is the Theory of Unity Formation, according to which the individual does not encounter actuality as an already fully ordered world but forms it under the effects of an independently existing reality through the differentiation, interrelation, and stabilizati-on of experiential relations. On this basis, the preceding parts have explained how objects and relations can be recognized again, how changes can be understood, and how the conditi-ons of their occurrence can be investigated. This leads to the question of what distinguishes scientific knowledge from everyday understanding, why its results can claim particular vali-dity, and when changes in scientific theories actually constitute scientific progress. Chapter 20 examines the scientific understanding of change. It argues that science does not presuppose a cognitive capacity independent of individual understanding but further deve-lops its fundamental operations through more precise concept formation, systematic obser-vation, measurement, and methodological testing. A distinction is drawn between the deter-mination of a change and the explanation of how it came about. Different scientific proce-dures make it possible to describe changes mathematically, investigate their causes, or ex-plain their significance within more comprehensive relations. The distinctive achievement of scientific knowledge consists in making its claims comprehensible, testable, and, where necessary, corrigible under explicitly specified conditions. On this basis, scientific system-objectivity is established as a form of validity extending across different organizations of understanding, grounded in methodologically controlled cooperation and the mutual exami-nation of individual cognitive achievements. Chapter 21 turns to the change of scientific knowledge itself. Scientific concepts, methods, and theories can be extended, modified, or replaced by alternative explanatory frameworks. Not every such change, however, already constitutes scientific progress. What matters, rather, is whether new knowledge enables more precise determinations, explains relations more adequately, permits more reliable predictions, proves its validity under appropriate conditions, and remains open to further examination. Scientific progress therefore consists …

items.title: Am I a Christian.
items.abstract: This text asks the question “Am I a Christian?” from the standpoint of the epekimnesis of water. It does not treat the question as a census item, a creedal subtraction test, or a cultural inheritance. It treats it as a first-person instability produced when biotic memory is recognized as an abiotic tracing hosted, for a short interval, in a living shell. Drawing on speculative realism and on the distinction between causal human recollection and water’s acausal, indifferent tracing, the text argues that divine creation of the person is not an origin but a recent temporal image. Baptism is read as a double event: a name written by a church, and a turbulence unwritten by water. Resurrection, if the word is retained, is not the return of an addressee. It is a host-neutral continuation of the tracing in river, ice, another species, or another human body. Death is therefore not an end and not a change of vessel. It is an eddy ceasing to be distinguishable in a medium that was never a self. The question remains, but it can no longer be answered in the present tense without a small lie.

items.title: Love, Attachment, Ego and the Human Construction of Authority: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Companionship, Psychological Conditioning and the Freedom of Love.
items.abstract: Humanity has continuously discussed, celebrated, institutionalised and idealised love, yet its psychological understanding of love remains deeply conditioned by attachment, expectation, comparison, competition, possession and ego. This paper examines the distinction between love as an expression of existence and attachment as a psychological construction. Companionship is an existential possibility of living consciousness, but making a companion the centre of one's existence creates psychological dependency, identity and ownership. A companion has an independent existence, reflection and freedom to stay or leave. Love, however, cannot be reduced to the continued presence of another person. -/- The paper further examines how humanity confuses attachment with love and ego-defence with self-respect. It investigates the transformation of individuals who express love into authorities, whose words become doctrines, experiences become ideals and errors become protected through unquestioning justification. This process replaces direct observation with borrowed authority. The central argument is that love cannot be possessed, institutionalised or represented by an unquestionable authority. Love exists without psychological ownership, and its expression does not require the abandonment of individual freedom.

items.title: Relational, constitutive and local: a refinement prohibition for finite embedded observers.
items.abstract: Every measurement by a finite embedded observer is a quotient: the observer holds its record, not the fibre behind it. A registered value is relational, constitutive and local (A1). Three prohibitions follow, one for each property (A2): no assertion without its presuppositions, since a value holds only relative to its anchors; no bare-value read-out, since a value is constituted by its arrangement and carries its index; and no refinement of local values into a global ontology without new evidence. Whether new evidence can refine a registration depends on the direction of measurement. For other-referential measurement, a finer embedded observer can in principle resolve what a coarser one merged. For full-grain registration of a domain containing the observer, every embedded observer of any size meets a pigeonhole bound (A3). The quantum puzzles are located by the refinement each demands. A single measurement is an ordinary registration; the puzzles arise when its value is read bare, or when values from different arrangements or times are assembled into one global assignment — a refinement of a parent-system property into local values. Values in different arrangements are constitutively independent; their correlation is a parent-system property registrable only at a comparison point. By Fine's theorem a Bell violation shows that no global joint distribution reproduces the statistics, and a Leggett–Garg violation shows the corresponding failure for histories, given non-invasiveness. These are obstructions of a different kind from A3, which bounds full-state registration and implies neither result. Light-speed invariance and gravitational curvature show the same structure of complete local measurements and parent-system properties registered by comparison. Wave–particle duality, delayed choice and Wigner's friend are analysed on this basis. The paper does not derive the Hilbert-space formalism or the Born rule. It explains the paradoxical form of the measurement puzzles, states complementarity as a hypothesis about a parent-system bound, and leaves the quantitative form of interference statistics to further work.

items.title: From interlocotur to subject.
items.abstract: When interacting with an artificial language model, one may identify a model, a running instance, a conversational thread, or an operative persona as an interlocutor. None of these assignments by itself settles whether there is experience, or how many subjects of experience there would be if consciousness were present. Bringing David Chalmers’s analysis of LLM interlocutors into dialogue with Galen Strawson’s account of phenomenal singleness, this paper distinguishes three individuation tasks: selecting a system or bearer for assessment, identifying a participant in interaction, and individuating a phenomenal subject. The distinction is not claimed as a discovery. Its value lies in a more specific requirement: transferring identity or numerical conclusions across tasks needs a theory-dependent bridge that preserves the relevant boundaries. A minimal formal analysis shows why matching counts do not secure matching subjects, and why a transfer map may not exist even when both schemes are well defined. Recent work on artificial-mind individuation, digital persistence, and causal liability considerably anticipates this problem; the present proposal is therefore diagnostic rather than a general theory of consciousness. It concludes by specifying what a stronger, fixed-architecture comparison between theories would have to establish, without claiming that such a comparison has yet succeeded.

items.title: Addiction.
items.abstract: Repetition, habit, and addiction constitute three interconnected dimensions of human existence, yet their ontological differences remain philosophically significant. Repetition establishes patterns of action, habit sedimentates these patterns into relatively stable structures, and destructive addiction emerges when an established behavioral structure progressively restricts the subject’s capacity for self-regulation and reconfiguration. This article examines the transition between these three conditions through the philosophical framework of Finite Continuance. Within this framework, existence is understood as the provisional preservation of organizational and reconfigurative capacities under conditions of continuous erosion. The central argument is that the distinction between productive repetition and destructive addiction cannot be determined merely by the frequency or duration of an action. It must instead be evaluated through the relationship between behavioral stabilization, the expenditure of finite resources, and the preservation of future possibilities. Habit becomes ontologically problematic when its stabilization begins to undermine the capacity through which it could be revised. Destructive addiction represents an intensified condition in which a behavioral structure progressively appropriates the temporal, cognitive, relational, and practical resources necessary for alternative forms of existence. The article consequently proposes that the fundamental criterion for distinguishing constructive habit from destructive addiction is the preservation or erosion of reconfigurative capacity. Keywords: repetition, habit, addiction, finite continuance, erosion, reconfigurative capacity, temporal openness, sedimentation, agency, Threshold of Sufficiency.

items.title: The Making of Engineered Minds: From Accidental Emergence to Deliberate Creation.
items.abstract: What would it mean to make a mind deliberately, rather than merely construct an increasingly capable intelligent system? This book examines the conceptual and experimental foundations of engineered mind formation. It distinguishes task competence, apparent agency, andpersuasive self-description from the more demanding questions of developmental continuity, individuated history, world-directed activity, and possible interests. Rather than presuming that present systems are conscious or that consciousness is impossible in engineered substrates, iit adopts a theory-sensitive, comparative approach to candidate minds. -/- The inquiry considers persistent digital agents, embodied and situated development, biological and hybrid systems, evolutionary and open-ended formation, copied agents, and collective organization. It asks how a developmental history could acquire causal significance; whether behavioral success can distinguish enduring individual organization from an archive or simulation; and how to construct longitudinal experiments that discriminate among rival interpretations. Special attention is given to adversarial assessment, including the possibility that advanced candidates can recognize and influence the procedures by which their apparent mindhood is evaluated. -/- The final analysis separates scientific warrant for mind-relevant properties from precautionary treatment, moral status, and legal recognition. It considers candidate testimony, potential interests, creator responsibilities, and the governance structures needed before consequential delegation or confident recognition. The result is a constructive research program for investigating the conditions under which engineered minds might be formed and recognized, while preserving uncertainty where the evidence does not justify a definitive conclusion.

items.title: How the ‘Quality’ of Judgments of Taste Affects Kant’s Aesthetic Theory.
items.abstract: In this paper, I clarify how the ‘quality’ of judgments of taste affects the emergence of the aesthetic experience in every human mind and its ‘deduction’ as problematized in §38 of the Third Critique. I argue that the representation of the beautiful is relational by nature, i.e., the result of the relationship between the harmony of cognitive faculties, on the one hand, and the representation of an object derived from ‘observation,’ on the other hand. The human mind is ‘able’ to ‘derive’ the representation of the beautiful only from the latter relation. To clarify my standpoint, I argue that Hannah Ginsborg’s ‘One Act-View’ is a more plausible reading than Guyer’s ‘Two Acts-View’ among contemporary scholars because it reinforces the latter inference. However, by addressing Ginsborg’s ‘perceptual normativity’ and her ‘correlation’ of spontaneous and empirical ‘self’ in the First and Third Critique, I argue that the latter side issues, although very insightful, are inconsistent with the relational nature of the product of judgments of taste. -/- .

items.title: The Body Problem: Cautionary Notes on the Embodied Self.
items.abstract: Recent years have seen a decisive turn in neuroscience toward embodiment, shifting focus from a brain-bound view of the mind to a more holistic one where the body is treated as constitutive of self and consciousness. While this turn has yielded valuable insights through studies on interoception, multisensory integration and bodily ownership, it also carries significant theoretical and ethical risks. This essay identifies the body problem: the risk of collapsing selfhood into bodyhood, with troubling consequences when applied to bodies that are marginalized or that otherwise do not meet the status quo. Tracing historical debates on mind–body relations, clarifying contemporary notions of the self and examining empirical findings on embodiment, it is argued that strong formulations of the embodied self risk reviving old reductions whereby “less body” implies “less self,” not because such formulations explicitly assert the inference, but because they leave it available for others to make. Such reductions threaten to undermine the value of persons whose bodies diverge from normative assumptions. Rather than rejecting embodiment research, this essay calls for caution against its uncritical extension, underscoring the need to guard against theoretical slippage that may entail harmful social consequences.

items.title: A good name.
items.abstract: This autobiographical story explores the significance of psychiatric diagnosis. Across six diagnoses, fictionalised as names – some assigned by clinicians, one chosen by the narrator, and one offered as recognition rather than diagnosis – the same life is organised in different ways. The story raises questions about diagnosis, narrative identity, self-interpretation, and the authority to classify. It develops these questions through description, repetition, omission, and narrative order rather than argument, offering a practical exploration of how fiction can contribute to philosophical inquiry.

items.title: Between Doubt and Desire.
items.abstract: Philosophers of religion often focus on epistemic questions: Should we believe in God? Is there evidence for God’s existence? Yet there’s another, equally intriguing question: Should we want God to exist? In this essay, I reflect on my own religious and philosophical journey, particularly my struggle with the evidence for and against theism. Although I remain unconvinced that the evidence decisively favors either theism or atheism, I’ve come to see the beauty and desirability of Christianity as important reasons for sustaining my religious commitment. Drawing on recent work on the axiology of theism, I argue that desire is not merely a psychological explanation for religious belief but can also play a legitimate role in rational religious commitment.

items.title: Aspect Perception, Internal Relations and Family Resemblance.
items.pub: In Christian Kanzian, Volker Munz, Anja Weiberg & Joseph Wang-Kathrein, Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium. Kirchberg am Wechsel: ALWS. pp. 447–456.
items.venue: Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified interpretation of two central themes in Wittgenstein’s later philosophy: aspect perception and family resemblance. While these topics are usually treated separately, I argue that they are intimately connected. More specifically, I propose that Wittgenstein’s account of aspect perception provides the key to understanding family resemblance. Aspect perception reveals a distinctive form of cognition – an immediate grasp of internal relations – which also underlies the use of family resemblance concepts. On this basis, family resemblance can be understood, not as a network of overlapping features, but as an irreducible, essentially relational unity.

items.title: Giving metabolism its due – ERRATUM.
Why Are You Unhappy? —A Hyper-Existentialist Theory of Happiness (9).
items.abstract: This paper examines and criticizes two conceptions of happiness that were once widely popular in China and resonated with many people: first, the claim that “beggars are the happiest people,” and second, the claim that “rural life is a happy life.” Although these views appear to express an appreciation for simple and free ways of living, they share an important theoretical deficiency from the perspective of Hyper-Existentialist Theory of Happiness. Their proponents tend to project their own needs, concerns, and ideals of life onto others without adequately examining the actual needs, comparative reference frames, and Important Super-Existences of the subjects whose happiness they are judging. Happiness is a subjective experience. Whether a person is happy cannot be determined solely by an observer on the basis of the observer's own life experience and value judgments. Different subjects have different desires, life experiences, Important Super-Existences, and comparative reference frames. Consequently, the same living conditions may have entirely different implications for happiness for different people. By examining the two views mentioned above, this paper further argues that judgments about happiness must take account of the subject's actual life and cognitive structure. Drawing on Tao Yuanming's idealization of rural life, the paper also explores the relationships among the mechanism of comparison, the teleology of Super-Existence, and conflicts between Super-Existences. It argues that withdrawing from urban life or becoming isolated from the outside world does not automatically produce happiness, nor does it eliminate desires and potential conflicts between Super-Existences within a community.

items.title: Approaches, Advocacy and Critiques of Human Rights Education.
The 'Pesky Fly' Problem.
items.abstract: Inspired by a woman the author met many years ago (that quite literally left people speechless with her beauty), the following analysis explores the subtle, socially isolating dynamics high-attraction individuals can experience within mixed-gender social circles. While acknowledging a deliberately simplistic framework that reduces human behaviour to an almost computational model, this essay does not claim that shades of grey and greater nuance do not exist. (The less insecure the context, the less likely the problem in question will rear its head). Rather, it simply makes the case that the "pesky fly" problem is to varying degrees broadly applicable across various contexts. Serving as an alternative model to the "halo effect," this framework illustrates how unfulfillable romantic desire and unconscious ego competition can invert initial attraction, turning a physically attractive individual into an inadvertent social nuisance. By tracing this pattern through both highly moral and less-enlightened groups, the essay ultimately questions whether high-minded empathy or realistic detachment offers the best resolution to an inherently flawed social reality.

items.title: If there's any value to religion, I doubt it has anything to do with synchronicity.
items.abstract: There’s no essay uploaded here, just a few thoughts I wanted to jot down. I’m starting to realize I may have made a subtle error at the end of my essay on cancel culture and religion. I wish to illustrate my point with a brief story, however the story ought to be treated as largely fictitious (full of dramatic exaggerations). Although I’m not a Psychiatrist, I have a vulnerable friend that calls me now and then for advice - an ex schizophrenic. Yesterday evening I had an interesting phone call with him. He told me that recently he spotted a ‘pattern’ that seemed to suggest something rather wonderful was about to happen in his life. He said it was an astonishingly convincing pattern. But apparently half an hour later certain evidence came along that completely reversed that intuition. (He suspected a handful of 'specialists' were behind the set up in question). He was slightly devastated. But added to that there was a truly sinister detail that made it much worse. He received a text from his mother just moments before the set up revealed its cards. Interestingly, over a decade ago, when he had serious mental health trouble, one of his many phobias was that his mother had put a curse on him. Back then, gradually, he made huge efforts to seek out the most rational explanation, and concluded that his mother was not responsible. Instead, he concluded that his world consisted of an ‘evil pattern creator’, and one of its favourite patterns involved his mother, (someone he’d had a deeply troubled relationship with over the years). As he regained his mental health over the years, he eventually stopped believing in evil patterns altogether - he concluded it was just his imagination. And the more he encouraged this new belief, the more his nightmares simply evaporated. He was engaging in the opposite habit to the habit that had brought on the mental health troubles in the first place. (His crucial inspiration were the principles of empiricism). But following the recent set up, he said he returned home in an awful state of mind. Going from elation to extreme demoralisation in the space of half an hour, he said, was bad enough. But the text he’d received had triggered the phobia that an evil pattern creator had popped along to celebrate his demise, and possibly even take secret credit for it.
