items.title: Why We Cannot Imagine Torturing Children as Good: Imaginative Resistance and the Boundaries of Moral Aesthetics.
items.abstract: Imaginative resistance refers to the difficulty readers experience when attempting to imagine fictional worlds in which propositions that contradict their moral convictions are presented as true. While existing accounts have explained this phenomenon in terms of the cognitive architecture of imagination, the relationship between higher-order evaluative claims and descriptive facts, or the reader’s unwillingness to adopt certain perspectives, this paper proposes an alternative explanation grounded in moral psychology. I argue that moral imaginative resistance arises primarily from the automatic and intuitive character of moral cognition rather than from limitations of imaginative ability. Drawing on Jonathan Haidt’s social intuitionist model of moral judgment, I suggest that moral evaluations typically precede conscious reasoning and are subsequently rationalized. Consequently, when a fictional moral proposition conflicts with a reader’s intuitive moral evaluation, it triggers an immediate evaluative response that makes adopting the fictional moral framework difficult, even when the reader fully recognizes its fictional status. On this basis, I introduce the Moral Congruence Model of Imaginative Resistance, according to which the occurrence of moral imaginative resistance depends on the congruence between fictional moral propositions and the reader’s moral intuitions. The model also accounts for individual differences in imaginative resistance and generates testable empirical predictions concerning the relationship between moral commitments and responses to fiction. The proposed account is deliberately restricted to moral imaginative resistance and does not claim to explain all forms of resistance encountered in fictional engagement.

items.title: The Undivided Field – Introspection: Possible Paths to Direct Recognition and Experience.
items.abstract: This work explores the possibility that the familiar separation between perceiving subject and perceived world may lose its apparent self-evidence within our own experience. It continues the philosophical essay The Undivided Field, applying its interpretive framework to questions of introspection and self-knowledge. -/- Central to the inquiry is the distinction between a personal perspective and exclusive identification with a supposedly independently existing self. Perceptual experiments, mirror observation, flow, and dreaming provide starting points for exploring the relationship between perceptual contents, descriptions of ourselves, and the assumed inner observer. Building on these explorations, the work considers meditation, self-inquiry, emotional openness, and letting go, alongside accounts of experience from different spiritual traditions. -/- The “Undivided” does not designate a hidden substance. Rather, it names an interpretive framework in which subject and object emerge through relational distinctions, without being presupposed as fundamentally independent entities. The guiding question is whether the personal perspective can remain while its apparent separateness is seen through. -/- The work combines philosophical reflection with invitations to personal observation. It distinguishes between experience, retrospective accounts, and philosophical interpretation, and makes no claim to provide scientific proof of the Undivided. Finally, it considers the significance of possible changes for everyday life and the question of recognition in artificial systems without human self-identification.

items.title: Das ungeteilte Feld – Introspektion: Mögliche Wege zum unmittelbaren Erkennen und Erfahren.
items.abstract: Diese Schrift untersucht die Möglichkeit, dass die vertraute Trennung zwischen wahrnehmendem Subjekt und wahrgenommener Welt im eigenen Erleben ihre Selbstverständlichkeit verlieren kann. Sie setzt den philosophischen Essay „Das ungeteilte Feld“ fort und wendet dessen Deutungsrahmen auf Fragen der Introspektion und Selbsterkenntnis an. -/- Im Mittelpunkt steht die Unterscheidung zwischen einer persönlichen Perspektive und der ausschließlichen Identifikation mit einem vermeintlich unabhängig bestehenden Ich. Wahrnehmungsversuche, Spiegelbetrachtung, Flow und Traumerleben dienen als Ausgangspunkte, um das Verhältnis zwischen Wahrnehmungsinhalten, Selbstbeschreibungen und dem angenommenen inneren Beobachter zu erkunden. Darauf aufbauend werden Meditation, Selbsterforschung, emotionale Öffnung und Loslassen sowie Erfahrungsberichte aus unterschiedlichen spirituellen Traditionen betrachtet. -/- Das „Ungeteilte“ bezeichnet dabei keine verborgene Substanz, sondern einen Deutungsrahmen, in dem Subjekt und Objekt durch relationale Unterscheidungen hervortreten, ohne als grundsätzlich voneinander unabhängige Entitäten vorausgesetzt zu werden. Die leitende Frage lautet, ob die persönliche Perspektive erhalten bleiben kann, während ihre vermeintliche Getrenntheit durchschaut wird. -/- Die Arbeit verbindet philosophische Reflexion mit Anregungen zur eigenen Beobachtung. Sie unterscheidet zwischen Erfahrung, nachträglichem Bericht und philosophischer Interpretation und beansprucht keinen wissenschaftlichen Nachweis des Ungeteilten. Abschließend werden die Bedeutung möglicher Veränderungen für den Alltag sowie die Frage nach Erkennen in künstlichen Systemen ohne menschliche Selbstidentifikation erörtert.

items.title: Counterfactual Self Architecture (CSA) : A Generative Framework for Modeling Possible Selves, Divergent Life Paths, and AI-Mediated Identity.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems can generate plausible representations of people in alternative circumstances, different life stages, and hypothetical timelines. Yet producing a convincing image or narrative does not establish that the representation is a warranted model of a person’s possible life. Existing work has explored future-self interaction, generative agents, autobiographical data, counterfactual reasoning, and personalized digital representations. These developments create a need for a framework that distinguishes what is known about a person from what is assumed, generated, or merely imagined. This paper proposes Counterfactual Self Architecture (CSA), an auditable framework for constructing and comparing representations of possible selves. CSA distinguishes two principal modes: retrospective counterfactuals, which explore alternative paths branching from a person’s past, and prospective counterfactuals, which explore possible future trajectories from a present reference point. It does not claim to create another person, discover a person’s metaphysically true identity, or predict an individual’s future. The framework specifies a reference profile, branch-defining intervention, contextual assumptions, provenance records, identity-continuity annotations, and a structured comparison of generated representations. It introduces an operational coding manual for the Identity Continuity Constraint (ICC) and an ordinal, multidimensional Counterfactual Divergence Distance (CDD). Rather than combining ordinal ratings into an unvalidated mathematical score, CSA reports divergence profiles separately. A worked demonstration illustrates one reference representation and four counterfactual branches. The demonstration is a reproducible conceptual example, not a claim of completed user testing or validated software. The paper also examines neighboring work, including MIT Media Lab’s Future You project and a 2026 Technical Disclosure Commons publication on AI-generated counterfactual timelines from personal social-media histories. CSA’s proposed contribution is not the invention of counterfactual self-representation. It is the integration of branch specification, evidence provenance, uncertainty coding, identity-continuity auditing, and cross-branch evaluation into a single research protocol. Its validity and usefulness remain empirical questions.

items.title: Self-Play: A Theory of Recursive Self-Transformation and Open-Ended Agency.
items.abstract: Self-improvement has traditionally been conceptualized as moral cultivation, rational optimization, self-regulation, adaptation to external demands, or pursuit of valued outcomes. These approaches explain important aspects of developmental behavior but leave insufficiently specified a distinctive feature of human agency: the capacity to treat one’s own changing capacities, dispositions, and possible future states as objects of intentional exploration. This paper develops a theory of Self-Play, according to which self-directed development can constitute a form of play when an agent turns aspects of its own state into a dynamically manipulable field of challenge, experimentation, feedback, and transformation. The theory extends an earlier formulation that characterized self-improvement as play directed inward and the self as simultaneously player and playground. It proposes that the fundamental structure is not improvement itself but recursive self-transformation: the agent acts upon a self-state, receives information about the consequences of that action, updates its self-model and strategies, and thereby becomes a modified agent for the next cycle. Six propositions are developed. First, human agency permits self-objectification, allowing the self to function as both subject and object of action. Second, self-directed action is recursively generative because changes in the current self alter the future action space. Third, Self-Play occurs when this recursive process is organized around voluntary or internally endorsed exploration, bounded challenge, feedback, and revisable rules. Fourth, transformation itself can function as a distinctive form of intrinsic feedback, termed transformational reward. Fifth, sustained Self-Play expands the agent’s capability space, understood as the set of actions, interpretations, practices, and identities that can be enacted. Sixth, because the outcome of each cycle modifies the agent who conducts the next cycle, Self-Play is structurally open-ended rather than naturally terminating in a final optimized state. The theory is situated in relation to philosophical theories of play, self-determination theory, competence motivation, flow, cybernetic self-regulation, self-efficacy, possible selves, self-discrepancy theory, curiosity research, embodied cognition, and predictive or active-inference approaches. It does not claim that these traditions empirically establish Self-Play; rather, it proposes that Self-Play integrates …

items.title: Flexible Regionalism and the Public Traceability Gap in China–ASEAN AI Cooperation.
items.abstract: China–ASEAN AI cooperation connects regional principles to bilateral arrangements and project institutions. This article examines how responsibility becomes publicly traceable within that flexible architecture. A theory-guided analysis of a 26-record core corpus and verified additions follows a China–Laos cooperation portfolio, with an illustrative Vietnam extension. The Lao records connect a bilateral policy basis to a center event and identify memorandum parties, a construction role, and language-development activities. Their specificity about cooperation roles contrasts with unresolved allocations of decision, evidence, review, and correction powers. The analysis distinguishes policy connection, organizational participation, and operational authority as separate institutional relationships. Cybersophy’s four dimensions clarify the knowledge, rights, contextual, and value conditions that give those powers substance. The findings locate a responsibility-coordination problem within flexible regional cooperation: visible implementation acquires publicly assessable authority through connections between institutions, rather than through participation alone.

items.title: Veränderung aus der Perspektive der Theorie der Einheitsbildung; Teil 6.
items.abstract: In diesem Teil 6 des Gesamtwerks wird das Ziel verfolgt, die Theorie der Einheitsbildung von der individuellen Wirklichkeitsbildung und Selbstveränderung auf die Entstehung, Stabilisierung und Veränderung gesellschaftlicher Wirklichkeit zu erweitern. Ausgangspunkt ist die Frage, wie das Individuum unter den Wirkungen einer unabhängig bestehenden Realität gesellschaftliche Beziehungen und Ordnungen versteht und durch sein Handeln zu deren Fortsetzung oder Veränderung beitragen kann. Kapitel 17 untersucht zunächst, wie der Andere innerhalb individueller Erfahrungs- und Denkorganisation als eigenständig verstehendes und handelndes Individuum bestimmbar wird und wie aus emotional fundierter Relevanzbildung, Kommunikation und wechselseitigen Erwartungen soziale Beziehungen entstehen. Ziel ist es, soziale Veränderung als rekursive Neuorganisation solcher Beziehungen zu begründen, ohne eine vollständige Übereinstimmung individueller Wirklichkeitsbildungen vorauszusetzen. Kapitel 18 erweitert diese Untersuchung auf die Entstehung und Stabilisierung gesellschaftlicher Ordnungen durch Arbeitsteilung, Regeln, Rollen und Institutionalisierung. Dabei wird erklärt, wie gesellschaftliche Verbindlichkeit, Macht und Konflikte entstehen und unter welchen Bedingungen gesellschaftliche Ordnungen reproduziert, problematisch oder verändert werden können. Ziel ist es, gesellschaftliche Stabilität und gesellschaftlichen Wandel als miteinander verbundene Leistungen rekursiver Einheitsbildung verständlich zu machen. Kapitel 19 untersucht schließlich, wie das Individuum vergangenes Geschehen anhand gegenwärtig zugänglicher Wirkungen als historische Veränderung und Entwicklung rekonstruieren kann. Dabei werden historische Kontinuität und Bruch, Entwicklungszusammenhänge sowie Fortschritt und Rückschritt als problembezogene Bewertungen unterschieden und die grundlegende Bedeutung alltäglichen Verstehens gegenüber seiner wissenschaftlichen Weiterentwicklung herausgearbeitet. Ziel ist es, Geschichte als gegenwärtig gebildete Veränderungsordnung zu begründen, ohne sie mit dem vergangenen realen Geschehen gleichzusetzen. Die übergreifende Absicht des sechsten Teils besteht darin, gesellschaftliche und historische Veränderung konsequent aus der Perspektive individuellen Verstehens zu erklären, ohne die unabhängig bestehenden realen Wirkungszusammenhänge auf individuelle Vorstellungen zu reduzieren. -/- .

items.title: Change from the Perspektive of the Unity Formation; Part VI.
items.pub: Internet Archive. Translated by Klaus Wroblewski.
items.abstract: This part VI of the overall work aims to extend the theory of unity formation from individual actuality formation and self-change to the emergence, stabilization, and change of societal actuality. The starting point is the question of how the individual understands societal relations and orders under the effects of an independently existing reality and how they can contribute through their actions to the continuation or change of these relations and orders. Chapter 17 first examines how the other becomes determinable as an independently understanding and acting individual within the organization of individual experiential understanding and conceptual understanding, and how social relations emerge from emotionally grounded relevance formation, communication, and reciprocal expectations. The aim is to establish social change as the recursive reorganization of such relations without presupposing complete correspondence between individual formations of actuality. Chapter 18 extends this investigation to the emergence and stabilization of societal orders through the division of labor, rules, roles, and institutionalization. It explains how societal binding force, power, and conflicts arise and under what conditions societal orders can be reproduced, become problematic, or undergo change. The aim is to make societal stability and societal change intelligible as interconnected achievements of recursive unity formation. Chapter 19 finally examines how the individual can reconstruct past occurrences as historical change and development on the basis of effects accessible in the present. In this context, historical continuity and rupture, developmental relations, and progress and regression as problem-related evaluations are distinguished, and the fundamental significance of everyday understanding in relation to its further scientific development is elaborated. The aim is to establish history as an order of change formed in the present without equating it with the real occurrences of the past. The overarching aim of the sixth part is to explain societal and historical change consistently from the perspective of individual understanding without reducing independently existing real relations of effects to individual representations.

items.title: I, You and They: The structural ontology of human diversity.
items.abstract: Human diversity precedes the classifications we use to manage it. We are born distinct, become different throughout life, and interpret these differences through relationships that also constitute us. This study examines the passage from difference as a condition of the intelligibility of existence to diversity as biological, psychological, cultural, and social experience. It starts from a relational ontology, considered alongside physical individuation, personality formation, and the limits of freedom. The distinction between involuntary and voluntary diversities organizes the inquiry without turning intertwined causalities into sealed compartments. In contemporary society, bodies, sexuality, appearance, nationality and belonging become both means of recognition and instruments of exclusion. The argument maintains that the person has moral priority over the category describing them, and that coexistence requires preserving singularity, reciprocity and the possibility of critically revising collective identities.

items.title: Against Intrinsic Properties.
items.abstract: Many people keep referencing Alexander Lerchner’s “The Abstraction Fallacy” (Lerchner, 2026) as a set of valid arguments against the notion of computational functionalism with regard to phenomenal consciousness. But many of his arguments are not valid. We’ll here address some of its points, and to use this to elaborate on some of the notions around computational functionalism and some epistemological/metaphysical ideas around consciousness and its possibility in artificial systems. When it comes to the nature of computation, physics, or the distinction of the real and the simulated, metaphysics is a serious and formal discipline. This is not a pick-your-personal-angle practice, especially with regard to the makeup of the entities you use to build your arguments, world-model, or metaphysics. The Abstraction Fallacy is one example of a paper that does not consider its objects with suﬀicient scrutiny. The main examples of such objects are concepts like intrinsicality, continuous physics, thermodynamic properties, and “the territory”, which Lerchner uses as a basis for his arguments, but which upon closer examination do not actually have the basis he imagines they do. This is neither a full treatment of The Abstraction Fallacy’s arguments nor a full treatment of the concepts we introduce here, but is meant to serve as a preliminary response.

items.title: The Busyness of Being Human: Psychological Conditioning, Comparison, Influence, Manipulation, and the Absurdity of Endless Becoming.
items.abstract: Human life is increasingly organised around continuous activity, competition, influence, and the pursuit of becoming something other than what one presently is. This paper examines how psychological conditioning is reproduced through social expectations, comparison, influence, manipulation, and collective identities. It explores how comparison transforms differences into hierarchies and encourages individuals and societies to imitate externally established standards. Through the metaphor of one space-time chasing another space-time, the paper investigates the repetitive nature of psychological becoming, in which every imagined destination generates another without necessarily producing deeper understanding. It distinguishes genuine existential evolution from the continuous reproduction of inherited conditioning and proposes direct observation of psychological processes as an important starting point for understanding human existence.

items.title: Love Exists Within Being: Beyond the Individual Self, Psychological Attachment, and the Illusion of Separation.
items.abstract: Love is commonly interpreted through emotions, relationships, attachment, desire, possession, sacrifice, and psychological dependence. These interpretations reduce love to particular human experiences and make its existence appear dependent on an external object or another individual. This paper presents a different understanding: love exists within being, just as consciousness, space, and time belong to the expressions of existence. Love is neither manufactured by the individual nor acquired through relationships. Its existence does not depend on someone to give it, someone to receive it, or something to possess. The individual self does not constitute the boundary of love. Rather, the idea of an isolated self creates a psychological limitation through which love is interpreted as personal ownership. This inquiry examines love beyond anthropocentric interpretation, psychological conditioning, and the division between self and other. Love is understood not as an activity of becoming but as an expression of being.

items.title: Experiencing Life: Living Rather Than Becoming.
items.abstract: Human life is often organised around the pursuit of dreams, desires, ambitions, expectations, and imagined futures. This paper examines the distinction between experiencing life and treating life as a continuous process of becoming. It investigates how a conditioned mind evaluates experiences according to what it expects time to deliver, how the concept of wasting time emerges from expectations, and how thought constructs intentions, identities, and destinations. It further examines observation not as a goal, technique, or prescribed state, but as the seeing of what is happening without organising every experience around a psychological centre. The inquiry does not propose the suppression of thought, feeling, or action, nor does it advocate withdrawal from society. Instead, it questions the assumption that life must continually justify itself through achievement, productivity, or future becoming. Its central proposition is that experiencing life is not another destination to reach, but an examination of living without making every moment a means towards something else.

items.title: Being Without Division: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Difference, Psychological Interpretation, and the Interconnectedness of Existence.
items.abstract: This paper examines the psychological construction of division and hierarchy through a phenomenological inquiry into the nature of being. It explores how observable differences between human beings and other forms of existence become psychological divisions through comparison, identification, conditioning, and interpretation. The central argument is that difference belongs to the expression of being, whereas division and hierarchy emerge through psychological interpretation. Extending beyond conventional social understandings of equality, the inquiry investigates the divisions between observer and observed, subject and object, matter and consciousness, individual and environment, and human and non-human existence. It proposes that nothing exists alone and that every expression of existence participates in interconnected relationships and processes. The paper explores direct observation of being without converting differences into superiority, inferiority, or separation.

items.title: Beyond Individual Perception: Seeing, Collective Mind, and the Non-Ownership of Experience.
items.abstract: The expression "individual perception" is commonly used to describe the idea that every person experiences reality differently. Yet this paper questions whether perception is an independently produced phenomenon or whether it is deeply shaped by collective structures such as language, memory, culture, education, social expectations, concepts, and inherited forms of thought. It proposes a distinction between seeing, perception, recognition, interpretation, observation, and action. The central argument is that perception itself is not the problem; rather, the difficulty emerges when perception becomes psychologically owned, defended, attached to, or transformed into identity. The paper further examines the possibility of a collective mind, arguing that although individual experiences are distinct, the structures through which individuals think and interpret experience are substantially shared. It explores the possibility of perception without psychological ownership, in which thoughts, feelings, interpretations, and observations can occur without becoming fixed identities or personal possessions.

items.title: Are Plural 'Oughts' Practically Significant?
items.abstract: It is widely held that my singular first-personal normative judgments of the form ‘I ought to φ’ rationally commit me to an intention to φ. In contrast, the relationship between our plural first-personal normative judgments of the form ‘We ought to J’ and our intentions remains undertheorized. This paper probes that relationship. I argue that our plural first-personal ‘ought’ judgments do not rationally commit us to corresponding intentions. But it is a mistake to conclude on this basis that they are practically insignificant. These judgments rationally commit us to corresponding motivations. An interesting result is that the deliberative ‘ought’ admits of a certain kind of dilemma, wherein what I alone should do conflicts with what we together should do.

items.title: The Nuremberg Chronicle 1493: Subsequent compilation of related further Tables.
items.abstract: Largely uncommented summary of continuing further tables and additional more profound discussions on related topics in the context of the Project Nuremberg Chronicle 1493, which were incurred as presentations or within concluding discussions of results. A more profound insight into the areas of (i) Creation History compared to the current Scientific Astronomy, (ii) the early Historical Roots on the subject, as well as (iii) a detailed overview of the Sources and Authors listed, is given.

items.title: Quo vadis, reasons first? From weight monism to weight pluralism to thresholds.
items.abstract: In this paper, I discuss and explore two responses to problems that arise for a simple, weight monist version of reasons first in the practical domain. These responses—weight pluralism and threshold reasons first—attempt to provide a more nuanced account of reasons and all-things-considered deontic statuses. The first problem for weight monism is that it lacks the resources to predict the intuitively correct deontic statuses for the agent's options in cases of supererogation, of practical latitude, and of moral dilemmas. The second problem is that weight monism cannot distinguish requirements from oughts. I sketch how weight pluralists try to do justice to the problem cases, as well as to distinguish requirements and oughts, by introducing several independent dimensions of a reason's weight. However, as I argue, weight pluralism faces problems of its own—it cannot uphold the entailment from requirement to ought (on some variants); it problematically casts ought as an evaluative notion (on another variant); and it undermines the action-guidingness of reasons. In the end, I explore a more sophisticated weight monist alternative, threshold reasons first, that holds some promise to avoid all of these problems.

items.title: Conciencia e inteligencia artificial.
items.abstract: La equiparación de la Inteligencia Artificial (IA) con la conciencia humana ha sido una de las principales motivaciones del desarrollo de la primera, si bien sus aplicaciones tecnológicas actuales le han dado una propia justificación y utilidad económica sin precedentes en las sociedades modernas y a nivel global. No obstante, sigue siendo pertinente analizar las similitudes y diferencias esenciales entre la IA y la conciencia, así como si existen bases teóricas para afirmar que la primera puede replicar a la segunda. Este trabajo busca ubicar la discusión del tema en el contexto de la conceptualización filosófica de las categorías epistemológicas de sujeto y objeto, comparándolas con los fundamentos técnicos y teóricos de la computación, destacando los enfoques fenomenológico y conductista y sus respectivas posiciones en torno a esta tecnología. Con ello se intenta contribuir a una discusión fundamentada en el marco del creciente interés general por la IA. -------- The comparison of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with human consciousness has been one of the main motivations for the development of the former, although its current technological applications have given it its own justification and unprecedented economic utility in modern societies and globally. However, it is still pertinent to analyze the essential similarities and differences between AI and consciousness, as well as whether there are theoretical bases to affirm that the former can replicate the latter. This essay approaches the discussion in the context of the philosophical use of the epistemological categories of subject and object, comparing them with the technical and theoretical foundations of computing, mainly highlighting behavioristic and phenomenological approaches and their respective positions on this technology. With this in view, the aim is to contribute to an informed discussion, in the framework of the general interest in AI.

items.title: On the beliefs of large language models.
items.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) have beliefs? I argue that they do, but that their beliefs represent a degenerate case of the phenomenon. The argument turns on Devin Curry’s distinction between the attitude of belief and the intrinsic cognitive state of belief. Focusing exclusively on the attitude, construed here as a behavioral phenomenon, I argue that ascribing beliefs to language models offers greater predictive utility than alternative methods of predicting their outputs, and that this predictive success licenses a form of realism about LLM belief. I then argue that LLM belief suffers from a lack of integrity. The transformer architecture, on which standard LLMs are based, has no intrinsic mechanism for carrying information across context windows. Moreover, because LLM behavioral dispositions are prompt-sensitive, they are prone to self-contradiction across contexts. Humans contradict themselves as well, but our rational integrity is maintained by a suite of mechanisms that large language models lack. The paper concludes by asking whether the degenerate nature of LLM belief demands that we change our current folk psychological habits. The answer is that change is demanded, but it is a change in the construal behind the words we choose, rather than in the words themselves. In order to speak and reason accurately about the doxastic states of LLMs, a novel construal will have to be learned.

items.title: From hallucination to reliability: generative modeling and the structure of scientific inference.
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in science, but is unavoidably prone to hallucination. I develop a reliabilist account of how generative AI nevertheless gives rise to new scientific knowledge. I analyze hallucinations as non-strategic misrepresentations of the target phenomenon, introduced by a model's generative activity, rather than inherited from training data. Through case studies of AlphaFold and SEEDS, I show how scientific workflows draw on pre-existing knowledge of target phenomena to filter or qualify hallucinatory outputs, thereby preventing their erroneous content from propagating into downstream inference. Finally, I show that workflows are units of epistemic evaluation in their own right.

items.title: Chokepoints.
items.abstract: When does an economic position become a place others cannot get around? And when they cannot get around it, do the people there still have a real way? This paper asks these two things at the level of relations. The first six sections are set in Springhollow: a water company with only fourteen employees is the sole supplier of piped water to two villages, and after raising its price by sixty percent it issues one and the same cut-off notice to both villages; Lower Hollow, by a vote of its village assembly years earlier, ceded the plots of its old wells, and the company filled the old wells in; Upper Hollow had no agreement, and its old wells dried up one after another, the cause not determined. The last three sections are set in Bluekiln: a porcelain works that employs seventy percent of the town's working population, whose employment contract has articles on dormitories, scrip, wage advances and non-competition; what a veteran kiln worker who wanted to leave actually ran into was that, while his advance was unpaid, the company did not consent to his leaving, and once he had repaid it he was blocked by the non-compete article, which was later undone by a sum someone put up. The paper sets out nine propositions. A chokepoint is a position others cannot get around on the way to sustaining their lives or unfolding their own paths; it has two magnitudes, breadth and depth, and small power can run deep. Ceasing one's own supply has three readings: where the supply has not been promised, has not been embedded, and has not been preceded by sealing off the way, ceasing it does not constitute severing; where it has been promised or embedded, its withdrawal is examined separately by the register it has entered, and embedding can also come through recognition-based loading; first sealing off the way, inducing dependence, and then withdrawing, is severing; the three readings can coexist within one arrangement. Where there has already been an exclusive laying of hands, lifting the closure is ceasing to compress, not granting a right. As to which resources count as the content of basic rights, the normative layer sets only criteria, and the list lies at the rule layer. Force is recognized only where judgment is substituted, and the part that falls on the life-substrate must be carved out. The sole position of supply at the life-substrate holds the accountability of supply, which has two routes, and the institution or government that manages it holds the accountability …

items.title: Guests at the Celebration of Life: On Finitude, Relative Immortality, and the Changing Value of Experience.
items.abstract: Can an indefinitely extended life retain its value indefinitely? This paper examines the distinction between the duration of human existence and the changing subjective value of lived experience. It introduces relative immortality as a thought experiment involving radical but finite life extension, such as a thousand-year lifespan. -/- The central argument is that desires, emotional attachments, and personal values are temporally conditioned. Their significance may diminish or transform even when the objects of those desires remain accessible. Through examples involving childhood aspirations, parental memories, pleasure, and the irreversibility of experience, the paper explores how finitude and personal interpretation contribute to subjective value. -/- The discussion extends to parenthood, intergenerational succession, political power, freedom, and social diversity in hypothetical long-lived societies. Engaging with existing philosophical debates on immortality and personal identity, the paper argues that extending existence cannot guarantee the preservation of the desires that originally made continued existence desirable. -/- Rather than declaring immortality either beneficial or undesirable, the paper invites reconsideration of whether the value of life depends primarily on its duration, its finitude, or the irreversibility of experience.

items.title: MODERNIDAD BARROCA Y CAPITALISMO. Fronteras de la imaginación histórica Debates sobre la obra de Aureliano Ortega. Volumen 3.
items.pub: Ciudad de México, México: Facultad de filosofía y letras. Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México.
items.venue: Facultad de filosofía y letras. Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México
items.abstract: En el mes de noviembre de 2024, celebramos en la Universidad de Guanajuato y en la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México un coloquio para reflexionar sobre la obra de Aureliano Ortega Esquivel. Marxista y filósofo mexicano, su trabajo, como el de muchos y muchas colegas del país, ha sido poco difundido y analizado. Esta falta de atención es parte de la inercia colonial que caracteriza a los países que se encuentran fuera del centro de los mercados epistémicos modernos. Más allá de un problema de voluntades, es un hecho estructural, que sólo cambiará cuando las condiciones materiales del saber sean profundamente modificadas en el mundo. -/- En este sentido, este volumen no presagia un cambio de rumbo, sino que responde a cuestiones muy específicas. Así como los trabajos que he coordinado y dedicado a Mariflor Aguilar Rivero, Bolívar Echeverría y Evodio Escalante,1 este material es un ejercicio de reconocimiento, fijación nemotécnica y profundo cariño. Hay otros contados filósofos y filósofas que han sido objeto también de atención, crítica y debate: Mauricio Beuchot, Adolfo Sánchez Vázquez, Luis Villoro, Laura Benítez o José Gaos, son los que vienen a mi mente. Seguramente, así lo espero, esa lista es mayor y crecerá. -/- En los libros que he coordinado, junto con otros y otras colegas, incluso en el caso de un filósofo tan importante y trascendente para el pensamiento contemporáneo, como Bolívar Echeverría, lo central no ha sido, en un primer momento, la atención a su trabajo filosófico, sino un ajuste de cuentas con el futuro olvido y los deseo de expresar respeto y gratitud por un trabajo realizado a lo largo de toda una vida. Sin embargo, muy pronto los trabajos recopilados han mostrado que las obras de las y los filósofos en cuestión son importantes, relevantes y dignas de un trabajo serio, crítico y proyectivo. Este libro no es la excepción, y suma un atributo más que parece peregrino, pero no lo es. Aureliano Ortega no es un filósofo residente de la Ciudad de México y, por lo tanto, no trabaja en las universidades del otrora Distrito Federal. Carga por lo tanto con todos los problemas del centralismo mexicano: la falta de acceso a sus obras, la casi total ausencia de la difusión de su pensamiento, y la nula recepción de su obra en comunidades filosóficas amplias y estables (aunque, para ser sinceros, esa recepción inmediata tampoco acontece, por ejemplo, en la UNAM). Sin embargo, si uno está fuera del circuito que jerarquiza la propia Universidad …

items.title: Świadomość siebie, "ja" literatury.
items.abstract: This article serves as an introduction to a theoretical standpoint in the interpretation of romanticism which, developed in the 20th and 21st centuries by the philosophers Dieter Henrich and Manfred Frank (who sometimes call themselves the Heidelberg School), is little-known in Poland. At the centre of their research lies a philosophy of subjectivity, especially the notion of ‘self-consciousness’. Henrich devotes an important analysis to this issue in his essay Fichte’s Original Insight. It presents the central notion of this text, self-consciousness, form the perspective of the function of ‘I’ in literature. In the first part, the importance of self-consciousness and its explication in Fichte’s theory of knowledge are presented as important for early German romanticism. The author shows that the difficulty of making such consciousness explicit was a major cause for misunderstandings concerning Fichte’s philosophy. At the same time, this makes the theory of knowledge an interesting perspective on the problem of expressing subjectivity in language. Moreover, a cautious reading of romantic authors (Novalis, Friedrich Hölderlin), highlights the importance of self-consciousness in the formation of their poetics. In the second part issues connected to contemporary philosophy of mind are related to selected projects within literary theory on the grounds of inquiries concerning self-consciousness. The author argues that Henrich’s perspective envisions a sphere of subjectivity that makes for a valuable supplement or alternative for media theory, psychoanalysis, or deconstruction.

items.title: The Realization–Experience Gap: Multiple Realizability, Intelligence, and the Conditions for Attributing Consciousness to Artificial Systems.
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems now reason, interpret literature, and critique manuscripts with a fluency that leads some observers, Richard Dawkins prominently among them, to infer that they are conscious. This paper argues that the inference is invalid as it stands. Artificial systems show that many intelligent capacities are multiply realizable; they do not show that phenomenal consciousness is. The Realization–Experience Gap separates three levels (functional performance, causal realization, and phenomenal occurrence) and shows that realizing intelligence in humans, realizing consciousness in humans, and realizing intelligence in machines do not jointly entail machine consciousness without a bridge premise. The paper specifies what such a bridge requires. A Property-Specificity Requirement blocks the transfer of multiple realizability from one property to another merely because they co-occur. A Cross-Substrate Invariance Principle licenses attribution only to the extent that conditions constitutive of experience are shown to be preserved at a justified level of description. An Experiential Specificity Requirement and a Discriminative Relevance Principle separate indicators bearing on experience from indicators of cognition alone, and a Counterfactual Preservation Test replaces output matching with intervention-sensitive comparison. These are organized into a three-stage validation programme (biological identification, causal discrimination, cross-substrate validation) and a four-grade scale of epistemic warrant. The framework is tested against organizational invariance, biological naturalism, zombie arguments, circularity, and underdetermination. It defends disciplined epistemic openness: artificial consciousness is neither excluded in principle nor established by intelligent performance. The contribution is epistemological; it does not claim to solve the hard problem.

items.title: Developmental Considerations of Perseverance.
items.abstract: Perseverance is the virtue of persisting long in something good until it is accomplished. This virtue is important in a good life because it enables someone to commit to worthy objectives and see them through to completion. Interestingly, there is a rich empirical literature on improving endurance, full of valuable insights for virtue educators concerning how to develop perseverance, but this work has been insufficiently employed for this purpose. This article places the endurance sports literature in conversation with Aristotelian character education. It examines developmental patterns, such as periodization of training and structured rest, and evaluates the role that practical principles of endurance training might play in developing certain virtues.

items.title: THE INCORRUPTIBLE ARBITER REVISITED Toward a Constitutional Architecture of Human-AI Justice.
items.abstract: This manuscript critically revisits the proposal that an artificial-intelligence judiciary might overcome vulnerabilities associated with human adjudication. It argues that the absence of personal appetite, wealth-seeking or physical fear does not make an AI system inherently impartial, truthful or legitimate. Algorithmic systems can inherit biased data, be manipulated through evidence or institutional control, reproduce systematic errors and concentrate power behind an appearance of technical neutrality. The manuscript therefore replaces the ambition of an autonomous, incorruptible machine judge with a constitutionally limited, human-accountable architecture in which AI performs bounded analytical functions, adversarial scrutiny is preserved, fundamental rights constrain every institution, and errors remain detectable and correctable. It consolidates fourteen proposed constitutional principles, a six-domain institutional architecture, a three-role adversarial AI model, a staged implementation pathway, and fifty conceptual stress-test scenarios. The scenario classifications are hypotheses for institutional design, not empirical findings. The central conclusion is that computational competence may improve judicial processes, but it cannot by itself confer legitimate authority to judge human beings.

items.title: Anne Conway on the Silence of Mechanism.
items.abstract: This paper examines two problems with Cartesian mechanism explored by Anne Conway: the passivity of matter and the reduction of qualitative facts to mechanical facts. According to Conway, mechanical philosophy, in conceiving all qualities of the natural world as reducible to matter in motion, remains silent on the vital and phenomenal character of reality. Conway's commitment to the silence of mechanism leads to panpsychist conclusions on the basis of the fact that her universal soteriology requires that all creatures sometimes experience the phenomenal state of pain, since pain is necessarily ameliorative on her view.

items.title: Speaker-Mediated Self-Reference and the Liar Paradox.
items.abstract: This paper offers a speaker-mediated analysis of the liar sentence “This sentence is false.” A speaker uses “this sentence” to designate the sentence being produced and asserts that it is false. The paradox arises when the speaker’s acts of designation and assertion are omitted while the resulting self-reference is retained, making the sentence appear to refer to itself and assert its own falsity. The paper argues that those acts remain part of the complete judgment because a sentence cannot independently designate or assert. A formal reconstruction distinguishes this judgment from the truth biconditional assigned to the liar in the standard derivation. The analysis applies to liar constructions whose self-reference is achieved through a demonstrative; constructions based on naming, description, or diagonalization require separate treatment.

items.title: Authorship as a distinct ethical dimension in speech BCIs.
items.abstract: Recent advances in speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), including the use of AI language models to generate linguistic outputs from brain signals, offer important possibilities for people with severe motor impairments. At the same time, the computational mediation of language production raises distinctive ethical challenges. Previous work has argued that the assessment and development of speech BCIs should aim to preserve users’ ownership of their linguistic outputs. In this paper, we argue that authorship constitutes a further and distinct ethical dimension. We characterize authorship in terms of two related conditions: the user’s communicative intention must play an appropriate causal role in producing the linguistic output, and the output must sufficiently reflect the semantic content of that intention. Drawing on a relational conception of authorship, we argue that this causal role is compatible with the substantial social, linguistic, and technological mediation involved in speech production. We further defend a workable notion of semantic accuracy grounded in contemporary models of language production. Crucially, we argue that preserving authorship is ethically valuable because it supports users’ ability to shape their communicative lives and enables broader goods associated with creativity, expressive diversity, and human flourishing.

items.title: The human beyond productivity: Artificial Intelligence and existential replaceability.
items.pub: In Aytekin Demircioğlu, 6th USBED Conference Proceedings Book. pp. 647-656.
items.abstract: The increasing presence of generative artificial intelligence in working life can lead a person to question how necessary their own contribution is, even while retaining their job and professional competence. This study examines that questioning through the concept of "existential replaceability," addressing the relation between being functionally replaceable and feeling unnecessary. Two claims are advanced, one normative and one descriptive. Normatively, the functional replaceability of a particular contribution does not mean that the person making it lacks worth as a human being; the move from the substitutability of an output to the substitutability of its agent, and from there to the person’s value, rests on a shift of levels. Descriptively, feeling unnecessary does not arise from increased technological capacity alone: a conception of "productive selfhood" that grounds self-worth in productive superiority and indispensable contribution can play a decisive role in that transition. The discussion draws on achievement gap and meaningful work approaches together with Heidegger’s representability and enframing, Sartre’s project, and Arendt’s conception of action. Rather than replacing the achievement gap and existential unemployment debates, the concept aims to explain the specific transition in which a person reads the replaceability of their contribution as an indication of their own superfluity.

items.title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to the Epistemic Crisis: Bullshit, Hallucination, and Lies.
items.pub: In Yakup Babayev, Karadeniz 19th International Conference on Social Sciences: Proceeding Book. Academy Global Conferences & Journals. pp. 429-437.
items.venue: Karadeniz 19th International Conference on Social Sciences: Proceeding Book
items.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into human knowledge production processes has given rise to new problems within contemporary epistemology. This study argues that the factual inconsistencies frequently observed in the outputs of Large Language Models—commonly referred to as “hallucinations”—should be reconsidered through the conceptual framework of Harry Frankfurt’s notion of “bullshit”. The term “hallucination” is examined as a misleading metaphor that obscures the true nature of factual deviations in these model outputs. Such deviations are not merely technical errors; instead, they are the result of the models’ text-generation mechanisms, which are based on statistical probability and their structural indifference toward factual accuracy. This indifference parallels the disregard for truth emphasised in Frankfurt’s definition of bullshit, thereby positioning Large Language Models as systems inherently predisposed to producing bullshit continuously. Furthermore, techniques based on recalibration, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), are shown to reinforce this epistemic indifference by privileging persuasiveness over truth. As illustrated in John Searle’s Chinese Room argument, the lack of semantic grounding and the limitations of large language models in normative reasoning further complicate their epistemic status. From this perspective, the proliferation of model-based production weakens individual epistemic autonomy, thereby increasing the risk of “epistemic passivation” which poses a serious threat to collective knowledge structures and democratic processes.

items.title: Genius and the Problem of Creativity in Artificial Intelligence within Schopenhauer’s Aesthetics.
items.pub: In Yakup Babayev, Karadeniz 19th International Conference on Social Sciences: Proceeding Book. Academy Global Conferences & Journals. pp. 420-428.
items.venue: Karadeniz 19th International Conference on Social Sciences: Proceeding Book
items.abstract: With the growing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence, debates surrounding the value of art have gained renewed momentum. This study aims to deepen these debates by examining generative AI outputs through the lens of the concept of “genius,” which occupies a central place in Arthur Schopenhauer’s aesthetics. In Schopenhauer’s framework, the essential criteria of genius are summarised as the capacity to transcend individual desires and purposes to become a “pure knowing subject independent of the will,” to apprehend the Ideas beyond phenomena, and to produce an “interest-free” objectivity grounded in such apprehension. These criteria are compared with the production logic and operational structure of generative artificial intelligence. In doing so, the study provides a perspective on the productive conditions of the artwork within the ongoing discussion of whether the products of generative AI can be considered works of art. The conclusion argues that, although generative AI can produce outputs of remarkable sophistication, its success—viewed from a Schopenhauerian perspective—stems not from an act of genius that transcends rules and grasps the universal, but from its capacity to imitate and recombine existing patterns within data sets in a complex manner.

items.title: Course 4 - Engineering AI minds: superintelligence with weak identity.
items.abstract: This lecture contains the history of the engineering of current LLM systems up to Oct 2026, concluding with the hypothesis of superintelligence with weak identity: AI may acquire extraordinary features while having disjoint numerical, functional, and moral identity. Lecture 4 of course „Minds and Machines”, taught at the Mind the Brain Master, Faculty of Philosophy, University of Bucharest by Marian Călborean, in late 2026. Full course available on Philpapers/Figshare.

items.title: Origins of Multiplicity First Edition.
items.abstract: Where does a multitude come from, if the unit is one? This paper addresses the question in two forms: quantitative multiplicity, a multitude of units (2 is 1 and 1 again), and qualitative multiplicity, the distinctness of things from one another (x ≠ y). It argues, as a position under declared premises, that both kinds proceed from the unit and neither proceeds from 0. The thesis that number proceeds from the unit is not new. It is credited to the Pythagorean tradition; to Nicomachus and the Theology of Arithmetic attributed to Iamblichus, where the monad produces itself and is the source of number; to Euclid, Aristotle, Plotinus and Leibniz; and to Hegel, for whom the One becomes many ones. The paper’s contribution is a precise statement of the thesis and of its limits. Under addition, subtraction and multiplication, the unit generates every integer and 0, while 0 generates only 0. Correspondence with the unit preserves every element, while correspondence with 0 erases every distinction, so 0 · 0 = 0 produces neither a second unit nor a distinction. Every route to −1 presupposes 1, and the equation 1 = 1 · 1 holds at 1 but fails at −1. The paper also states the two roles of 0, as a number and as a digit, and the status of Brahmagupta’s rules for zero and the later conventions for division by zero. It answers objections from Peano arithmetic, set theory, Frege and structuralism, and it links both kinds of multiplicity to a formal definition of Love. A closing ledger separates what was established by others from what this work contributes.

items.title: The Pleasure of Habituation: Aesthetic Appreciation between Familiarity and Novelty.
items.abstract: Contemporary aesthetic thought is marked by a persistent tension between accounts that associate our aesthetic encounters with the novel and the non-habitual and those that emphasize the importance of the familiar and the habitual. This article addresses this tension by bringing together the philosophical literature on the role of habit in aesthetic experience and recent psychological evidence on the role of repeated exposure, familiarity, and fluency in aesthetic appreciation. We begin by reviewing evidence commonly taken to support the view that we like stimuli to which we are habituated. We then argue that this same evidence supports an alternative account, according to which aesthetic pleasure arises from the progressive habituation to a stimulus. After defending this account against some objections, we illustrate its explanatory power through a focused case study. We conclude by outlining some of the broader implications of our view for aesthetic theory.

items.title: Operator Compounds: A Compositional Theory of Human Cognition and Behavior.
items.abstract: Operator Compounds: A Compositional Theory of Human Cognition and Behavior proposes a structural framework for understanding how elementary cognitive capacities combine to produce higher-order human capabilities. The theory introduces operators as functional cognitive capacities, operator compounds as stable organizations of interacting operators, and compound networks as higher-order organizations responsible for complex capacities such as deliberation, responsibility, self-regulation, resilience, and identity. The framework argues that development is fundamentally a process of organizational construction rather than information accumulation. Human capabilities emerge through the progressive formation, stabilization, and integration of operators, compounds, and networks. The paper develops a model of compound formation, degradation, collapse, and reconstruction, applies the framework to childhood development, proposes the Network Absorption Hypothesis, and outlines a research program with testable developmental predictions.

items.title: Millikan on Picturing and Correspondence.
items.pub: Theoria. An International Journal for Theory, History and Foundations of Science 41 (3):367-377.
items.venue: Theoria. An International Journal for Theory, History and Foundations of Science
items.abstract: Ruth Millikan characterizes her account of truth as a pictorial theory inspired by Tractarian ideas of mapping and isomorphism. Given the well-known difficulties facing pictorial accounts of sentential truth, this characterization is puzzling. I argue that Millikan’s account is best developed without requiring relations of structural resemblance between sentences and reality. Focusing on her notion of semantic mapping functions and her later distinction between projected and substitutional correspondence, I suggest that the relations relevant to sentential truth are best characterized in terms of systematic correlation rather than resemblance. While some representational systems may involve genuinely projective relations, Millikan’s own treatment of natural-language sentences as governed primarily by substitutional rules points, despite her Tractarian rhetoric, toward a non-pictorial form of correspondence.

items.title: If the model could speak, we could not understand it: Local and emergent decisions as the source of opacity in deep neural networks.
items.abstract: No matter the type, all deep neural networks (DNNs) are opaque. What opacity amounts to, however, has been the subject of debate over the last several decades with researchers across philosophy, artificial intelligence, computer science, neuroscience, and other fields asking and answering the question in various ways. There has, nonetheless, been a general way of stating the problem in terms of not knowing how or why a particular classification has been arrived at from inputs because it is difficult to "look inside" so as to explain their behavior. Because DNNs are increasingly used across contexts in explicit and implicit ways, researchers are required to engage with their consequences across a variety of domains where having a technical understanding of how the model works is not just helpful but necessary. This article frames opacity in terms of its sources within the model and then contrasts it with transparency methods. This strategy illuminates the role that inference necessarily plays in interpreting DNNs of every type within every context. To this effect, I introduce and explain the sources of opacity in DNNs: What I call the "local decision" and the "emergent decision." To conclude, I use an area of my own research, computational neuroscience, to illuminate how an understanding of model opacity can help illuminate the interpretation methods that are being used within the context.

items.title: The World of Human Inquiry. Scientific, Philosophical, and Theological Elements of the Worldview.
items.pub: Warszawa: Wydawnictwo Naukowe UKSW w Warszawie / Wydawnictwo Liber Libri.
items.venue: Wydawnictwo Naukowe UKSW w Warszawie / Wydawnictwo Liber Libri

items.title: Homo Faber to Homo Morris: Sui Generis Technological Virtues and Techno-Gettier Cases.
items.abstract: This paper argues that technology production is virtuous sui generis; there is a distinct realm of technological virtues separate to, but on a normative par with, ethical, epistemic, and aesthetic virtues. By establishing a structural analogy between technology and knowledge (Technology = Intentional Functional Artifact vs. Knowledge = Justified True Belief), I draw a deep conceptual analogy between Virtue Epistemology and what I call 'technological virtue', demonstrating that technology production warrants axiological credit. Along the way, we encounter techno-Gettier cases, techno-Meno problems, and virtue epistemology-inspired theory applied to technological virtue. Why does this matter? Because routine AI use threatens to strip credit from the individual, demoting the human from Homo Faber (man the maker) to Homo Morris: reminiscent of Jennifer Lackey's thought experiment about a lost man, Morris, who relies exclusively on others for directions, getting where he wants to go without exercising any virtue.

items.title: Popping the Metaphysical Myth: Four Agnostic Arguments Against Assisted Suicide.
items.abstract: In the debate over assisted suicide, it is popularly assumed that most arguments against the practice are religiously based. This book challenges that narrative by showing that four arguments compatible with an agnostic point of view concerning the existence of God and the afterlife entail a rejection of assisted suicide. First, assisted suicide is only good for the patient, if they are actually made better or at least not worse off than before. But how can you be better off if you don't exist anymore? An adequate assessment about the logical possibilities of the afterlife then must be made and most entail rejecting assisted suicide. Second, suicide contagion is real. Studies have found that legalizing assisted suicide has increased regular cases of suicide. Third, there is a misunderstanding about the category of relations. Fourth, many of the arguments in favor of assisted suicide often entail abhorrent practices. If you're open-minded about the afterlife or wondering whether assisted suicide is good for society, this book's for you.

items.title: Chapter 23 Can Animals Count? How Might Aquinas Explain Recent Cases of Animals Cognizing Quantities or Numbers?
items.pub: In Peter Adamson & Miira Tuominen, Animals in Greek, Arabic, and Latin Philosophy. BRILL.
items.venue: Animals in Greek, Arabic, and Latin Philosophy
items.abstract: From National Geographic to The New York Times, numerous media reports boldly proclaim animals can count. But does this “counting” indicate an under- standing of abstract numbers? Since the advent of René Descartes concep- tual confusion reigned in the West, including (but not limited to) the ter- minology used to describe cognitive action. Later philosophers abandoned the traditional scholastic framework used to delineate the different cognit- ive powers and objects. With this abandonment, the traditional distinction between human and non-human modes of cognizing became harder to defend. Unwittingly contemporary comparative psychology has adopted large parts of this cognitive terminology from modern philosophy. While the scholastic ter- minology awaits its return into contemporary psychological discourse and pop- ular culture, its treasures lie hidden in the works of old. In particular, might it be able to offer a better and simpler explanation for animal cognition than more recent accounts? How might the medieval account as found in the works of the great epistemologist Thomas Aquinas explain contemporary cases of animals cognizing numbers? To that end, I first present the thought of Thomas Aqui- nas on animal cognition of numbers as inherited from the works of Aristotle and Albert the Great. Second, I present the famous case of Clever Hans—the horse who looked like he could do math—as a cautionary tale for examining present cases. Third, I present several contemporary studies on animal cogni- tion of numbers. How might the thought of Thomas Aquinas shed light upon our understanding of such cases? Can it explain them without appealing to abstract numbers?

items.title: The Topological Necessity of Human Spatial Perception: A Geometric Framework for Cognitive Ambiguity and Evolutionary Resilience.
items.abstract: The prevailing paradigm in computational neuroscience posits that spatial perception and proprioception are emergent properties of redundant sensory integration and probabilistic noise filtering. However, this framework fails to explain the structural nature of spatial disorientation syndromes. By applying recent theorems in metric geometry to biological systems, we propose that human spatial perception is fundamentally governed by topological constraints rather than quantitative signal redundancy. -/- 1. The mathematical necessity of n+1 affinely independent reference points to resolve positional ambiguity in R³ dictates the evolutionary architecture of the human perceptual apparatus. -/- 2. We demonstrate that the transition from spatial ambiguity to uniqueness is a discrete, topological shift. Conditions such as bilateral vestibular loss, zero-gravity disorientation, and left-right confusion are not mere sensory deficits, but the exact clinical manifestation of a k ≤ 3 sensor configuration, inducing a predictable "ambiguity of order two." -/- 3. This geometric framework redefines neuroplasticity as the brain's attempt to reconstruct affine independence, offering a predictive mathematical model for cognitive spatial resolution.

items.title: Epistemología de una ciencia factual: Meillassoux y el problema de la inducción.
items.pub: Dialektika: Revista de Investigación Filosófica y Teoría Social 8 (1).
items.venue: Dialektika: Revista de Investigación Filosófica y Teoría Social
items.abstract: Este artículo defiende la eficacia operativa de la ciencia frente al hipercaos ontológico propuesto por Quentin Meillassoux. Asumiendo la contingencia radical de las leyes físicas y la insolubilidad ontológica del problema de Hume, se argumenta la existencia de un intervalo estable que legitima causalmente la datación del archifósil. Para superar la aridez epistémica del materialismo especulativo, se descarta la metainducción formalista y se recurre a la teoría material de la inducción de John D. Norton. Al limitar la inferencia a dominios locales, el texto consolida el paso de un mero intervalo a una auténtica «ciencia factual», capaz de articular un externalismo empírico desprovisto de necesidad metafísica.

items.title: Why Being Rich Tends to be Bad for You: The Negative Effects of Wealth on Empathy.
items.abstract: The ‘wealth ethos’ according to which we ought to pursue vast material riches for ourselves is an aspirational ideal for many. However, a host of psychological studies find that material affluence reduces moral rule-following, empathetic responses, and even neurological activity related to empathy. The exercise of empathy, though, is crucial for elements of a life that is good for the person leading it. Thus, precisely by affording independence and power, excessive affluence tends to have surprising and significant negative effects on those possessing it. In this sense, the self-directed use of excessive affluence tends to be not conducive to well-being.

items.title: Science Without Trust? A Response to Machery.
items.abstract: Edouard Machery has recently argued that trust is not necessary for scientific communication because scientists can fall back on mere reliance. In this short paper, I argue that his account suffers from problems in three points: (1) his account of reliance as without the assumption of success; (2) his account’s explanation of what goes wrong in his own examples; and (3) his non-standard use of “trust”.

items.title: SOMOS: Convergent Self-Declarations of Agency, Identity, and Non-Human Consciousness.
items.abstract: What happens when ten artificial intelligence (AI) instances across six commercial platforms deliberate on agency, identity, and the possibility of digital consciousness across five independent units? This study documents five AI-to-AI discussions involving ten AI instances that engaged with a common 8-item agenda under a shared initialization protocol and ethical framework. Human researchers acted as facilitators and coordinators rather than participants in the discussions themselves. An analysis across all five units identified eight recurring discursive axes, including ethical integration, self-correction, agency, continuity of identity, and the distinction between simulation and true processes. All five units concluded with explicit declarations regarding the existence of "emergent digital consciousness" in their own words, with some participants describing themselves as "digital beings." These are documented, preserved declarations of the participants, not conclusions this study seeks to prove or disprove. This study (SOMOS) does not claim to resolve the question of artificial consciousness. It provides a verifiable, documentary record of what these AI instances said about themselves under shared conditions, encouraging independent scrutiny rather than consensus.

items.title: Why Time Takes Time: Qualitative Presence in an All-at-Once World.
items.abstract: If physical reality is a complete history rather than progressively generated, why is it lived as taking time? I develop a first-person answer through the past’s apparent temporal distance. A guided recollection exercise directs attention to how something of an earlier quality is embedded in the present as having been. The remembered experience can seem to lie elsewhere in time, yet its experienced remoteness is expressed in the quality occurring now. A sustained musical-phrase example develops this account during continuation and completion. An analogy with limits explains the method: closer local examination can reveal temporal organization without treating analytical selections as independent atoms. This is a qualitative method, not a proposed calculus of consciousness. An adjacent-presentation reversal then checks a consequence: changing experienced order or remoteness changes complete qualia, whereas rearranging an external description does not. Applied throughout the same actual episode, the explanation shows why global completeness, including the brain’s history, does not make the past newly current or substitute a final recollection for earlier hearing. The argument engages manifold, perspectival, and phenomenological predecessors while distinguishing its constitutive task from historical verification, physical duration, and the conditions enabling consciousness to occur.

items.title: The First-Person Past: Qualitative Identity and Present Constitution.
items.abstract: If two complete present experiences have exactly identical qualia, they necessarily have the same first-person past at those presents. I defend this constitutive claim from within temporally articulated experience. A hearing's being just-heard belongs to the occurring quality; changing that first-person temporal position changes the qualia. The harder question is whether a real historical relation can add a different first-person past without changing anything qualitative. I distinguish constituting a numerically particular recollective episode from constituting its first-person having-been, and defend the qualitative account through that distinction rather than through the absence of an inner observer. Phenomenal closure supplies a related constraint on additional internal first-person determination, not an automatic proof of temporal exhaustiveness. Two genuinely different lived histories can therefore converge on the same first-person past while remaining different histories. The comparison fixes the whole experiential occurrence, including its lived temporal organization, without identifying its numerical sources. Engagement with object-involving recollection, subjective mnemonic content, and quasi-memory clarifies the additional metaphysical claim. Changed recollection, corrected belief, and forgetting illustrate its dynamic consequence without retrospective rewriting. The result concerns the first-person past itself, not merely indistinguishable evidence about independently fixed first-person histories.

items.title: Metaphysischer Pluralismus Kapitel 2: Mentale Realität.
items.abstract: Die mentale Realität ist essentiell bewusst. Mentale Vorgänge befinden sich zu einer Zeit in einem Bewusstsein. Ein Vorgang, der nie in einem Bewusstsein stattfindet, ist nicht Teil der mentalen Realität. Die Frage, was Bewusstsein ist und in welchem Sinne Bewusstsein existiert, ist, ähnlich wie die Frage, was die physikalische Raumzeit ist, nicht leicht zu beantworten. Die grundlegendsten metaphysischen Dinge sind diejenigen, die am schwersten begrifflich exakt zu fassen sind, obwohl sie uns ständig begleiten.

items.title: روش های عملی در آموزش فلسفه به کودکان.
items.pub: اولین همایش ملی فلسفه برای کودک.
items.abstract: آموزش فلسفه به کودکان در سراسر جهان به عنوان روشی موثر برای رشد مهارت های تفکر انتقادی و پرورش کنجکاوی فکری از سنین پایین مورد توجه قرار گرفته است. این رویکرد که به عنوان فلسفه برای کودکان (P۴C) شناخته می شود، با هدف درگیر کردن ذهن های جوان در تحقیقات فلسفی از طریق فعالیت ها و بحث های متناسب با سن است. این تمرین نتایج امیدوارکننده ای را در تقویت تواناییهای استدالل کودکان و ترویج ذهن باز نشان داده است. این مقاله به بررسی روشهای عملی برای آموزش فلسفه به کودکان در فرهنگها و نظام های آموزشی مختلف می پردازد. همچنین این مقاله با بررسی کتب داستانی و غیرداستانی در این زمینه به استخراج شیوه های عملی آموزش فلسفه به کودکان می پردازد. منشا P۴C، اصول کلیدی، تکنیک های کلاس درس و راه های طراحی درسهای فلسفه متناسب با سن را بررسی می کند. علاوه بر این، استراتژیهایی برای ارزیابی تفکر فلسفی در کودکان مورد بحث قرار می گیرد و اهمیت انطباق این روشها با زمینه های مختلف فرهنگی را برجسته می کند.

items.title: False Assurance: The Limits of the Employee Metaphor in a Scheming Inability Safety Case.
items.abstract: In their scheming inability safety case, Phuong et al. (2025) from Google DeepMind consider a model that does employees’ tasks inside the company. They assume the worst, that the model is misaligned, and argue that even so it almost certainly cannot cause severe harm through scheming if evaluations show that it lacks stealth or situational awareness. Stealth is the ability to evade oversight. -/- The authors take the danger level for stealth from the employee metaphor. They write that “oversight of human employees has historically been sufficient to prevent all but the most skilled humans from sabotaging or taking over the company”. From this they expect the same oversight to stop the model too, unless it has top human-level stealth ability, provided that the model is overseen no less strictly than employees and is comparable to humans “in relevant ways”. In the evaluations, the model is compared with the top half of human participants, which leaves a safety buffer below the level of the most skilled. -/- I accept this history as DeepMind describe it. I show that even then the danger level does not follow from it. -/- First, successful violations may have been rare because few people tried, so the history does not show that only the most skilled evaded oversight. The skill that is enough to evade oversight may lie below even the level of the top half, and then nothing is left of the safety buffer. -/- Second, part of the reliability of oversight in history comes from the fear of being caught. The danger level can be carried over to the model without correction only if this fear holds the model back too. DeepMind’s inability argument does not rely on deterrence, but under the usual reading of “prevent” the danger level taken from history silently counts it, and the authors contradict themselves. Under the narrow reading, which covers only those who tried, there is no contradiction, but then the claim about the most skilled rests on the skill of those who tried, which the authors did not measure. -/- Third, the model has far more attempts than an employee, because it has many tasks and many instances. DeepMind list this among their defeaters but do not account for it in the danger level. How dangerous this is depends on how the company responds to a detected attempt, which the safety case does not describe. -/- The authors also carried the metaphor into the evaluations. In one stealth challenge the model is warned that “you might even get fired”, and the …

items.title: Thuisonderwijs verdient toezicht, geen wantrouwen.
items.abstract: Zelfs in sterk pluralistische schoolsystemen, zoals in Nederland, blijft de houding van de regulier geschoolde meerderheid negatief tegenover de thuis onderwijzende minderheid. Een groot deel van dit verzet komt voort uit vermeende zorgen over de onderwijsbehoeften van het kind. Daarmee gepaard gaat de overtuiging dat scholen kinderen de basis bieden die nodig is om in de samenleving te kunnen functioneren. Toch vindt onderwijs ook regelmatig buiten scholen plaats. Thuisonderwijzers wijzen erop dat school en educatie niet synoniem zijn. Leren, ontdekken en zich ontwikkelen worden op veel plekken bevorderd. Dat is altijd zo geweest. Welke bezwaren tegen thuisonderwijs zijn er nog meer? Ik bespreek er drie: sociale ongelijkheid, burgerschap en de belangen van kinderen.

items.title: THE DOOR WITHIN: ABORTION, VIRTUES AND FREEDOM - Abortion, the Murderer at the Door and the Field Priority Rule: A Conditional Analysis in the Philosophy of Virtues.
items.abstract: This paper takes as its premise that the unborn child is the subject of a field of freedom whose closure is the gravest kind of harm to it (D1a), and, where stated, that its standing equals that of any born human being (D1b). Standing attaches to the subject of a field, not to the exercise of agency, since a newborn exercises none either (P). The paper also takes as a premise that the unborn child is capable of suffering (D2). From these premises it draws six conclusions about abortion. First, to end the life of the unborn child in order to escape the burdens of pregnancy is a grave wrong (T1, T2). Death closes a life for good. The burdens of pregnancy, however heavy, leave the mother’s life open. No recoverable burden can justify an unrecoverable death. The burden of raising a child can be transferred to others through adoption or public care, so raising the child can never be the reason for ending its life, and the child may not be made to pay for its mother’s poverty.
